tools.name: mcp__plugin_context-mode_context-mode__ctx_fetch_and_index
tools.description:
Fetches URL content, converts HTML to markdown (JSON is chunked by key paths, plain text indexed directly), persists it in a searchable knowledge base, and returns a small preview window per source. The raw page bytes never enter your conversation — they live in storage and you retrieve any section on-demand via ctx_search.

Caching: every fetch is cached on disk and reused for repeat calls within the TTL window. The default TTL is 24 hours; override per-call with the `ttl` parameter (milliseconds, `ttl: 0` bypasses cache like `force: true`). Stored content older than 14 days is cleaned up on startup.

WHEN:
  - You need web content (docs, changelogs, API references, spec pages) and the raw page bytes should NOT enter your conversation
  - Multi-URL research (library evaluation, migration scans, doc comparisons): pass the `requests` array and a `concurrency` value 2-8 for parallel I/O
  - You want repeat lookups against the same URL to be cheap (TTL cache hits return only a hint, no re-fetch)
  - You want a long-lived cache window (override `ttl` upward for stable specs) or a guaranteed-fresh fetch (`ttl: 0` or `force: true`)

WHEN NOT:
  - You already have the content locally — store it via the inline index tool
  - The page is SPA-rendered (JavaScript-required to materialize content) — this is a plain HTTP fetch, no headless browser

RETURNS:
  Per-source preview windows extracted around indexable headings plus indexing metadata (chunk counts, source labels, cache state). Raw content is NOT echoed back — retrieve any section on-demand via ctx_search(source: "<label>"). Concurrency parallelizes the fetch phase up to your chosen value (capped by the host's logical CPU count); the FTS5 write phase always runs serially because SQLite is a single-writer store. Net latency = max(fetch latency across the pool) + sum(per-source index write time). Cache hits skip both phases and return a small freshness hint instead of re-fetching. Use 4-8 for stable I/O-bound batches; lower the value when the target host enforces a per-IP rate limit you cannot raise.

EXAMPLE: ctx_fetch_and_index(
  requests: [{url: "https://react.dev/...", source: "react"}, {url: "https://vuejs.org/...", source: "vue"}],
  concurrency: 5
)

url.description: Single URL to fetch and index (legacy single-shape)

source.description: Label for the indexed content when using single `url` (e.g., 'React useEffect docs', 'Supabase Auth API'). For batch, put source in each requests entry.
Label for this URL's indexed content

requests.description: Batch shape: array of {url, source?} entries. Use with concurrency>1 for parallel fetch. Each request indexed under its own source label. Output preserves input order.

concurrency.description: Max URLs to fetch in parallel (1-8, default: 1). Use 4-8 for I/O-bound multi-URL batches (library docs, changelogs, pricing pages). Capped by os.cpus().length on small machines (response notes when capped). Indexing is always serial regardless — only fetches race.

force.description: Skip cache and re-fetch even if content was recently indexed

ttl.description: Override the cache freshness window for this call, in milliseconds. `ttl: 0` bypasses the cache like `force: true`; omit to use the default 24h TTL.

tools.name: DeferredToolPlaceholder
tools.description: Reserved placeholder that keeps deferred tool loading active; never call this tool.

tools.name: mcp__plugin_context-mode_context-mode__ctx_search
tools.description:
Search a unified knowledge base with a multi-strategy ranking pipeline. Two parallel matchers run on every query: a Porter-stemming matcher ("caching" finds "cached", "caches", "cach") and a trigram-substring matcher ("useEff" finds "useEffect"). Their ranked lists are merged via Reciprocal Rank Fusion, so a document that ranks well in both surfaces above one that wins only on a single strategy. Multi-term queries get an additional proximity-rerank pass that boosts passages where the query terms appear close together. Typos are corrected via Levenshtein distance and re-searched. Result snippets are window-extracted around the matched terms, not blindly truncated.

The knowledge base is unified: queries reach indexed content you stored (ctx_index, ctx_fetch_and_index, ctx_batch_execute output) AND auto-captured session memory written by hooks (decisions, errors, blockers, plans, user prompts, rejected approaches, tool failures, compaction guides — 26 event categories). File-backed sources carry a content hash and auto-flag staleness when the source file changes.

WHEN:
  - You want to recall something that exists in storage (recently indexed content, prior session events, auto-memory) instead of re-reading raw sources
  - You have multiple related questions about the same body of knowledge — batch every question into one call (the ranking pipeline runs per-query but the round-trip cost is paid once)
  - You want to scope the query to one labelled source (pass `source` — partial match is fine)
  - You want a chronological view across current session + prior sessions + persistent auto-memory (pass `sort: "timeline"` — the default `relevance` mode only ranks within the current session)
  - You want to filter ranked results by content shape (pass `contentType: "code"` to surface implementation snippets or `contentType: "prose"` to surface explanations)

WHEN NOT:
  - The data you want to query has never been stored in the knowledge base AND no session memory has accumulated around it — capture first (run a gather-and-index call), then come back here to query
  - You have one ad-hoc question against data that is not in the knowledge base — answer it inline by running code in the sandbox tool; one round-trip instead of capture-then-query

RETURNS:
  Per-query ranked sections with window-extracted snippets. Use 2-4 specific technical terms per query. Common session-memory source labels: `decision` (user corrections / preferences), `error` and `error-resolution` (past failures + their fixes), `blocker`, `plan`, `user-prompt`, `rejected-approach`, `compaction` (post-compact session guide). See ctx_stats for live category counts.

EXAMPLE: ctx_search(queries: ["root cause", "proposed fix", "test coverage"], source: "issue-#683")
EXAMPLE: ctx_search(queries: ["what did we decide about caching"], source: "decision", sort: "timeline")
EXAMPLE: ctx_search(queries: ["useEffect cleanup pattern"], source: "react-docs", contentType: "code", limit: 5)
EXAMPLE: ctx_search(queries: ["last user prompt", "active skills", "open blockers"], sort: "timeline")

queries.description: Array of search queries. Batch ALL questions in one call.

source.description: Filter to a specific indexed source (partial match).

contentType.description: Filter results by content type: 'code' or 'prose'.

sort.description: Sort mode. 'relevance' (default): BM25 ranked, current session only. 'timeline': chronological across current session, prior sessions, and auto-memory.

content.text: Tool loaded.

lastPrompt: rerun the failing CI and merge when CI is green

### Code Health – How easy is your code to maintain and evolve?[¶](#code-health-how-easy-is-your-code-to-maintain-and-evolve "Link to this heading") > The Code Health profile and main KPIs[¶](#the-code-health-profile-and-main-kpis "Link to this heading") > Advanced: How is the weighted average calculated?[¶](#advanced-how-is-the-weighted-average-calculated "Link to this heading")

### Advanced: How is the weighted average calculated?[¶](#advanced-how-is-the-weighted-average-calculated "Link to this heading")

The code health scores are aggregated by a weighted average. The weight is the number of lines of code (LoC) in each file. That way, a file with 5000 LoC carry more weight than a small file with 100 LoC. This provides a more accurate aggregated score. Consider:

Let’s say we have three files:

1.  a.c: code health 2.0, LoC 5000 (a massive problem)
    
2.  b.c: code health 10.0, LoC 100 (small and simple)
    
3.  c.c: code health 10.0, LoC 10 (even smaller and simpler)
    

Calculating a pure average gives a code health of 7.33 which is high and non-representative.

However,a weighted average gives a code health of 2.18 which is much, much more representative of the codebase as a whole.

### Module Smells[¶](#module-smells "Link to this heading")

*   **Low Cohesion**: Cohesion is calculated using the LCOM4 metric. Low cohesion means that the module/class has multiple unrelated responsibilities, doing too many things and breaking the Single Responsibility Principle.
    
*   **Brain Class aka God Class**: A Brain Class is a large module with too many responsibilities. A module is a Brain Class if 1) it’s a large module with many lines of code, b) it has many functions, and c) at least one Brain Method.
    
*   **Developer Congestion**: Code becomes a coordination bottleneck when multiple developers need to work on it in parallel.
    
*   **Complex code by former contributors**: If the developer behind a hotspot with low code healt leaves the organization, the maintenance risk increases significantly.
    
*   **Lines of Code**: Large files receive lower code health.

### Function Smells[¶](#function-smells "Link to this heading")

*   **Brain Method aka God Function**: A complex function/method that centers the behavior of the class/module and becomes a local hotspot.
    
*   **DRY (Don’t Repeat Yourself) Violations**: CodeScene detects duplicated logic that is actually changed together in predictable patterns.
    
*   **Complex Method**: Many conditional statements (e.g. if, for, while) leads to lower code health. Measured using cyclomatic complexity.
    
*   **Primitive Obsession**: Code that uses a high degree of built-in, primitives such as integers, strings, floats, often lacks a domain language that encapsulates the validation and semantics of function arguments.
    
*   **Large Method**: Large functions with many lines of code are generally harder to understand.

# Code Health – How easy is your code to maintain and evolve?[¶](#code-health-how-easy-is-your-code-to-maintain-and-evolve "Link to this heading")

Code quality issues cost time, money, and missed deadlines. It’s vital to know when you can safely move ahead and implement new features versus when you might have to take a step back and improve what’s already there. That way, your system remains maintainable. CodeScene’s Code Health metrics lets you strike that balance:

*   Code Health makes code quality objective rather than subjective.
    
*   Code Health is the only code-level metric in our industry with a proven link to speed and quality.
    
*   In tandem with Hotspots, Code Health provides the quality dimension when prioritizing technical debt or looking for refactoring opportunities.
    
*   Allows you to identify by short-term risks, as well as tracking long-term trends via multiple high-level KPIs.
    
*   Fully transparent – all issues are reported in our Virtual Code Review.
    
*   Actionable: Code Health issues come with automated refactoring recommendations, and future degradations are prevented via CodeScene’s IDE integration and/or PR Quality Gates.

--- [current-session | 2026-11-09 19:45 | cs-code-health::https://codescene.io/docs/guides/technical/code-health.html] ---

### What happens to disabled rules?[¶](#what-happens-to-disabled-rules "Link to this heading")

*   Disabled rules are no longer be part of the code health calculation. This means the reported code health can look better than the initially reported baseline.
    
*   Disabled rules will not be presented in the virtual code review.
    
*   Disabled rules will not be supervised as part of the delta analysis and PR quality gates.

### Function Smells[¶](#function-smells "Link to this heading")

*   **Brain Method aka God Function**: A complex function/method that centers the behavior of the class/module and becomes a local hotspot.
    
*   **DRY (Don’t Repeat Yourself) Violations**: CodeScene detects duplicated logic that is actually changed together in predictable patterns.
    
*   **Complex Method**: Many conditional statements (e.g. if, for, while) leads to lower code health. Measured using cyclomatic complexity.
    
*   **Primitive Obsession**: Code that uses a high degree of built-in, primitives such as integers, strings, floats, often lacks a domain language that encapsulates the validation and semantics of function arguments.

### Implementation Smells[¶](#implementation-smells "Link to this heading")

*   **Nested Complexity**: This is revealed as if\-statements inside other if\-statments and/or loops, and is a construct that significantly increases the risk for defects.
    
*   **Bumpy Road**: A bumpy road is a function that fails to encapsulate its responsibilities, leading to code containing multiple logical chunks of logic. Just like a bumpy road will slow down you driving, a bumpy road in code presents an obstacle to comprehension. There’s also an increased risk for feature entanglement. The remedy is often to extract and encapsulate the chunks of logically dispersed behaviors in their own functions.
    
*   **Complex Conditional**: A complex conditional is an expression inside a branch (e.g. if, for, while) which consists of multiple, logical operators such as AND/OR. This makes the code hard to understand.
    
*   **Large Assertion Blocks**: A test-specific code smell. Blocks of large, consecutive assert statements indicate a missing abstraction.
    
*   **Duplicated Assertion Blocks**: A test-specific code smell. Indicates a DRY violation as the same assertion block is copy-pasted across a test suite.

## Disable Local Smells via Code Comment Directives[¶](#disable-local-smells-via-code-comment-directives "Link to this heading")

CodeScene lets you disable function level smells via directives provided as source code comments:

// @codescene(disable:"Complex Method")
void execute(ProgramOptions\* options) {
   // ...lots of complex code here...
}

The disable option instructs CodeScene to ignore the Complex Method code smell on that function. You can disable multiple code smells in the same directive:

// @codescene(disable:"Complex Method", disable:"Bumpy Road Ahead") <-- look, two disabled smells
void execute(ProgramOptions\* options) {
   // ...lots of complex code along a bumpy road...
}

A short cut for disabling all smells is the disable-all directive:

// @codescene(disable-all)
void execute(ProgramOptions\* options) {
   // ...lots of complex code along a bumpy road...
}

The code health directives have a few simple rules:

*   The @codescene directive supports all function smells. You cannot use them to disable file level issues (e.g. Lines of Code, Low Cohesion).
    
*   A directive _always_ applies to the function/method following it.
    
*   Code Health directives can be part of a larger, multi-line comments (e.g. /\*\* comment blocks \*/ in Java).
    
*   The string in the disable instruction has to be an _exact_ match of the code smell name seen in the virtual code review. Unknown or misspelled directives are ignored.

CodeScene’s code health rules are calibrated against real-world codebases. As such, the default rules represent the state of the art when it comes to predicting maintenance and delivery risks. No matter your current Code Health level, you never want it to become worse. Once code has degraded in health, it’s expensive to bring it back on track. For that purpose, CodeScene alerts on any declining code health:

![CodeScene alerts on any declining code health.](../../_images/code-health-decline-alerts.png)

Fig. 51 CodeScene alerts on any declining code health.[¶](#code-health-decline-alerts "Link to this image")

The rules for the various alerts are:

*   _Declining Code Health_: Raised when a file shows a declining code health trend so that its score is now lower than it was over the past year. Note that we use a threshold to avoid raising alerts for minor fluctuations: the code health has to decline by at least 0.1.
    
*   _Predicted Decline_: Think of this as an early warning. We notify you when a file with recent development activity starts a downwards slide that is noticable, but not yet severe enough to cause a Declining Code Health alert.
    
*   _File climbs on the hotspot ranking_: This alerts you to a file which sees an increasing amount of development activity **and** is declining in Code Health. It’s a severe warning since the file is likely to become a future source of high-interest technical debt.

# Axis review: are the 5 axes sufficient? Should `calls_per_edge` become the 6th?

This document records a deliberate review of archy's score axes after the v0.20 promotion of `cc_mean` to `complexity`. The two questions are independent and the answers diverge.

**TL;DR**

- The 5 current axes (modularity, acyclicity, depth, equality, complexity) are sufficient for what they measure. A real but narrow gap exists; it is coupling-strength and type-coverage shaped, not call-density shaped.
- **`calls_per_edge` should not be promoted to a 6th axis.** It passes the orthogonality check but fails the directionality, actionability, and discriminant-validity checks an OECD-style composite indicator requires.
- The best candidate if a 6th axis is ever added was **type-hint coverage** (Python-specific, clear direction, cheap to compute, actionable). **Empirics ran in 2026-05** and concluded against shipping it in any form: independence is the weakest archy has measu
- The right home for call-graph data is **a refinement of the existing modularity axis** (call-weighted Newman Q) and **agent-navigation MCP tools** (already shipped). Neither requires a new axis.

The detailed argument follows.

## The question

The v0.16 introduction of `calls_per_edge` as a diagnostic, and the strong orthogonality numbers it produced on the 27-project benchmark, set up an implicit expectation that it would be promoted to a score axis "at a deliberate version boundary." After `comple

There are actually two questions here:

1. **Sufficiency.** Are the 5 current axes catching the structural pathologies a Python codebase can fall into, or are there meaningful gaps?
2. **Specifically `calls_per_edge`.** Even if there are gaps, is `calls_per_edge` the right signal to fill any of them?

The answers below treat them separately.

## What each existing axis catches, and what it doesn't

| axis | catches | misses |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **modularity** | community structure of the import graph (Newman Q) | nothing about call intensity within communities |
| **acyclicity** | fraction of nodes inside cycles (Tarjan SCC + tangle ratio) | nothing about near-cycles or back-edges that carry heavy traffic |

"""The `archy diff --strict` verdict: no new cycles, no new layer violations,
and no weakened rule in archy.yaml.

A ratchet for codebases that already carry findings. `archy cycles --strict`
fails on day one for most existing projects (25 of 28 bench graphs have a
cycle), so the likely response is to delete the gate. This one keeps every
finding the committed baseline already records and fails only on what is new.

**What counts as a new cycle (SCC-subset rule, #521).** A current cycle is
carried when, after ignoring modules the baseline never saw, what remains sits
inside ONE baseline cycle. So shrinking, splitting or renaming within a tangle
passes, a new file joining one passes, and a new import between two modules
already in the same tangle passes. A cycle fails when it forms among modules
that were outside every baseline cycle, when it pulls an existing acyclic
module into a tangle, or when it merges two baseline tangles.

The rejected alternative, keying on edges inside a cycle, would also fail a
new import between two members of one tangle. In a legacy tangle such as
django's 157-module SCC, those imports are routine edits, so that key fires
exactly where the ratchet is meant to stay installed.

"Ignoring modules the baseline never saw" needs the baseline's module list,
which snapshots record since `--strict` shipped. A baseline without one cannot
tell a new file from an existing module, so the verdict is refused rather than
guessed.
----

Any uncommitted changes are also included.

# How CodeScene's `cs` judges code health, and what archy could take from it

Fact-gathering date: 2026-11-09. Sources: `cs docs` (CLI, v as installed), the
CodeScene [Code Health guide](https://codescene.io/docs/guides/technical/code-health.html),
`cs rules-config list-thresholds --language python`, and probes run against
synthetic Python files and archy's own `src/`. Every number below was read from
the tool or measured, not recalled; where it is the vendor's claim rather than
ours, it says so.

## What `cs` measures

A file gets a score from 1 to 10 (10 is healthy). The score falls with each
**smell** found in it. Three families (vendor docs):

- **Function smells:** Complex Method (cyclomatic complexity), Large Method,
  Brain Method, Excess Number of Function Arguments, Primitive Obsession,
  String Heavy Function Arguments, Code Duplication.
- **Implementation smells:** Deep Nested Complexity, Bumpy Road Ahead (several
  separate nested blocks in one function), Complex Conditional (several
  boolean operators in one condition), plus test-only Large and Duplicated
  Assertion Blocks.
- **Module smells:** Lines of Code in a Single File, Number of Functions in a
  Single Module, Low Cohesion (LCOM4), Overall Code Complexity, Overall
  Function Size, Brain Class.

Aggregation (vendor docs): a project score is a **LoC-weighted average** of its
file scores, because a plain mean hides one huge bad file (their example: 2.0 at
5,000 LoC plus two tiny perfect files is 7.33 plain, 2.18 weighted). CodeScene
reports two KPIs, **Hotspot Code Health** (weighted over the files that change
most) and **Average Code Health** (all files), because a healthy average can
hide a bad hotspot.

Enforcement (vendor docs and CLI): `cs delta <base>` compares the working tree
or a branch with a base and reports degraded, improved and fixed issues per
file. It exits 0 unless `--error-on-warnings` is passed. A "declining" file is
one whose score fell by at least 0.1. Customisation is two-layered:
`.codescene/code-health-rules.json` (a weight per rule from 1.0 down to 0.0, a
numeric threshold per metric, rule sets matched by path glob) and a
function-level source comment `@codescene(disable:"Complex Method")` that
cannot suppress file-level smells.

## Exact Python defaults (read from `cs rules-config list-thresholds`)

| Smell | Threshold |
|---|---|
| Complex Method | cyclomatic complexity 9 (alert at 100) |
| Large Method | 70 lines (alert at 500) |
| Excess Function Arguments | more than 4 (constructors: more than 5) |
| Deep Nested Complexity | nesting depth 4 |
| Bumpy Road | 2 bumps, each at nesting depth 2 |
| Complex Conditional | 2 branches (alert at 10) |
| Lines of Code in a File | 600 warn, 3,000 alert, 6,000 critical |
| Mean cyclomatic complexity of a file | 4 |
| Code Duplication | functions of 10+ lines, 75% similar |
| Primitive Obsession | 30% of a file's function arguments |
| Large assertion block (tests) | 4 consecutive asserts |

## Probes (synthetic files, `cs review --output-format json`)

All matched the table: 5 sequential `if`s is clean and 8 fires Complex Method;
4 arguments is clean and 5 fires; a 60-statement function is clean and 70 fires
Large Method; nesting 3 is clean and 4 fires; a condition with two `and`s fires
Complex Conditional and one with a single `and` does not; two separate
`for`/`if` blocks fire Bumpy Road. A file needed roughly 600 lines of code to
earn Low Cohesion and 1,000 lines of code to earn Lines of Code in a Single
File; around 333 functions earned Number of Functions in a Single Module.
Probes that did **not** fire: a 16-line duplicated function pair (below the
10-line, 75% rule's effective bar for our shape), Primitive Obsession on four
tiny functions, and Low Cohesion on a two-group eight-line class.

Command surface worth knowing: `cs review FILES --output-format json` returns
`{path, score, review[]}` per file with `category`, function names and line
ranges, which is easy to script. `cs check FILE` prints lint-style
`warn: file:line: Smell (detail)` lines. `cs delta main` prints per-file
before and after scores and, usefully, the metric and threshold behind each
change ("cyclomatic complexity from 23 to 10, threshold = 9"). `cs review`
needs `cs auth` and does not run offline. It refuses a directory outside a git
repo for `delta` only.

## archy's own code, scored (51 files in `src/archy`, before any refactor)

Mean 8.58 over 48 scorable files, 32 below 10. Worst: `conventions.py` 2.93,
`cli_render.py` 3.59, `cli.py` 4.40, `graph.py` 4.44, `mcp_runs.py` 4.60,
`layers.py` 4.85. Warnings across `src`: 109 Complex Method, 81 Bumpy Road, 48
Excess Arguments, 32 Complex Conditional, 14 Deep Nested, 13 Large Method, 4
Low Cohesion, 3 file length, 2 Duplication.

## Overlap with what archy and ruff already do

- **Cyclomatic complexity:** archy already computes it per function
  (`archy.complexity`). Flagging archy's cyclomatic at or above 9 on `src/archy`
  gives 112 functions against `cs` Complex Method's 109, **92 of them the same
  function**; the exact value differs by 1 to 4 for most (68 of 92), so the two
  count different constructs. ruff's `C901` at `max-complexity = 8` finds only
  39, so it is a different, smaller measure and not a stand-in.
- **Arguments, branches, statements:** ruff has `PLR0913` (55 at `max-args = 4`),
  `PLR0912` (10) and `PLR0915` (2). These are the same niche as the archy
  value-prop note in `AXIS_REVIEW.md` (type-hint coverage was ruled out because
  mypy and pyright own it); function-level size rules are owned by linters.
- **Churn weighting:** archy already ranks files by cyclomatic complexity times
  git churn (`archy hotspots`, `what-to-refactor-next`), which is CodeScene's
  hotspot idea.
- **Ratchet on new findings:** `archy diff --strict` already fails only on
  findings that are new relative to a committed baseline, for cycles and layer
  violations.

## What is genuinely missing in archy

1. Per-file aggregation: no file-level score, no LoC-weighted project number, no
   hotspot-weighted versus all-files split.
2. The composite smells ruff has no rule for: Bumpy Road, Brain Method, Low
   Cohesion, Overall Code Complexity, module and file size.
3. A delta gate on **changed files' health**, not only on structure.
4. A rules file with per-metric thresholds, path-scoped rule sets and a
   function-level suppression comment that stays visible in the output.

## What this document does not claim

- That any of these smells predicts defects or agent success. The vendor claims
  a link to speed and quality; that is theirs, unverified here, and archy's own
  record is that every pre-registered claim it measured came back null
  (`WHAT_DIDNT_WORK.md`).
- That archy should add a sixth score axis. Any new indicator would face the
  OECD four-condition check in `AXIS_REVIEW.md` first, and the likely home is a
  diagnostic next to `hotspots`, not the composite.
- That the threshold table transfers: it is CodeScene's calibration, read from
  its CLI, not archy's.

content.text:
CI is green on both open PRs, with all 21 checks passing and no new CodeScene comments on either.

**#868 (conventions.py refactor).** CodeScene flagged three new deep-nesting issues, in helpers I had extracted. I flattened them with three small helpers: `_assigned_names`, `_base_names` and `_registry_call`. The `cs review` score for the file is now 3.98, up from 2.93. Full gates pass locally (pytest 2047). An AST comparison against `main` shows only the same four functions changed. I did not re-run the DeepWork review after this last fix.

**What `cs` checks.** It scores each file 1 to 10 from smells at three levels:
- **Function level:** complexity, length, argument count and duplication.
- **Implementation level:** nesting, "bumpy road" (several separate nested blocks in one function) and complex conditions.
- **Module level:** file size, function count and cohesion.

The project number is weighted by lines of code, and it is reported separately for the most-changed files. `cs delta` compares against a base branch. I read the exact Python thresholds from `cs rules-config list-thresholds` and reproduced them with probes. For example, cyclomatic complexity of 9 or more, more than 4 arguments, more than 70 lines, nesting of 4, and 2 or more bumps. File-length warnings start at 600 lines, but my synthetic files never triggered that smell, so I couldn't confirm that threshold. The full write-up is `docs/research/CODESCENE_HEALTH_MODEL.md` in #869, and its probe claims are corrected.

**How it compares with archy.** archy's existing cyclomatic count at 9 or more flags 112 functions on `src/archy`, against 109 from `cs`. 92 are the same functions, so Complex Method is mostly reproducible already. ruff's `C901` finds only 39, so it isn't a stand-in. What archy lacks is file-level aggregation, the composite smells ruff has no rule for, a changed-files gate, and tunable thresholds with suppression.

**Tickets filed.**
- **#870:** research ticket with pre-registered thresholds. It must report before anything else is built, since every claim archy has measured so far came back null.
- **#871, #872, #873:** `archy health` (a per-file smell report plus project numbers), a gate on changed files, and tunable thresholds plus suppression comments that are always reported. All three are blocked on #870, and none is a new score axis.
- **#874:** a duplicated loop in `conventions.py` that the review found outside my diff.
- **#867:** a test gap I found earlier.

Two things to flag. A chained command in my shell script pushed #869 before I'd fixed its first draft, which had three wrong claims about the probes; the corrected version is in the PR now. `conventions.py` also got longer in lines (1003 to 1066 by `cs`'s count), so reaching its file-length smell needs a module split, not more function extraction.

I haven't merged either PR. Which one next: merge #868 and #869 first, or carry on with the next file (`cli_render.py` at 3.59)?

            lines.append(f"  {'':<28}     {c.name} = {dist}  ({c.setters} of {b.count} set it)")
    return lines


def _registry_lines(report: ConventionsReport, top_n: int) -> list[str]:
    lines = [
        "",
        "## registries - values declared by repeated construction "
        + _shown(len(report.registries), top_n),
    ]
    if not report.registries:
        lines.append("  (none)")
    for r in report.registries[:top_n]:
        lines.append(f"  {r.constructor:<28} {r.count:>3} @ {r.home_module} ({r.home_count})")
        if r.literal_names:
            shown = ", ".join(r.literal_names[:6])
            more = f" (+{len(r.literal_names) - 6})" if len(r.literal_names) > 6 else ""
            lines.append(f"  {'':<28}     names: {shown}{more}")
        for c in r.keyword_defaults[:3]:
            dist = ", ".join(f"{v}x{n}" for v, n in c.distribution)
            # "13 of 80 pass it" is the fact; a bare distribution reads as if the
            # whole family were declared that way, which inverts the meaning of
            # an argument that is usually left at its default.
            lines.append(f"  {'':<28}     {c.name} = {dist}  ({c.setters} of {r.count} pass it)")
    return lines


def _gap_lines(report: ConventionsReport) -> list[str]:
    lines: list[str] = []
    if report.export_gaps:
        lines += [
            "",
            f"## export gaps ({len(report.export_gaps)}) - defined but not re-exported "
            "beside their siblings",
        ]
        for g in report.export_gaps:
            lines.append(
                f"  {g.export_module:<28} {g.family}: {g.exported}/{g.defined}"
                f"  missing {', '.join(g.missing)}"
            )
    if report.doc_gaps:
        lines += [
            "",
            f"## doc gaps ({len(report.doc_gaps)}) - public members their own docs do not name",
        ]
        for g in report.doc_gaps:
            lines.append(
                f"  {g.doc_root + '/':<28} {g.family}: {g.documented}/{g.defined}"
                f"  missing {', '.join(g.missing)}"
            )
    return lines


def _surface_lines(report: ConventionsReport, top_n: int) -> list[str]:
    lines = [
        "",
        f"## surfaces {_shown(len(report.surfaces), top_n)} - wire all of these together",
    ]
    if not report.surfaces:
        lines.append("  (none)")
    for s in report.surfaces[:top_n]:
        where = s.module or "across modules"
        lines.append(
            f"  {s.kind:<8} {s.stem:<28} {s.surface_count} @ {where}: {', '.join(s.surfaces)}"
        )
    return lines


def _gate_lines(report: ConventionsReport) -> list[str]:
    # The question this section exists for is "should MY NEW FINDING gate?", so
    # a finding-failure exit and a bad-input exit must not share a count.
    optional = [g for g in report.gates if g.optional]
    codes = ", ".join(str(c) for c in report.gate_codes) or "none literal"
    lines = [
        "",
        f"## gates ({len(report.gates)} finding-failure exit(s), "
        f"{len(optional)} caller-controlled; exit code(s): {codes})",
    ]
    if not report.gates:
        lines.append("  (none: no finding in this project fails the build)")
    return [*lines, *(_gate_row(g) for g in report.gates)]


def _error_lines(report: ConventionsReport) -> list[str]:
    kinds = ", ".join(
        f"{kind}={sum(1 for g in report.errors if g.kind == kind)}"
        for kind in sorted({g.kind for g in report.errors})
    )
    where = ", ".join(sorted({g.module for g in report.errors}))
    return [
        "",
        f"## errors ({len(report.errors)} user-error exit(s) - bad input, not a finding)",
        f"  {kinds} @ {where}" if report.errors else "  (none)",
    ]


def _model_lines(report: ConventionsReport) -> list[str]:
    m = report.models
    bases = ", ".join(f"{b}={n}" for b, n in m.base_counts[:5])
    return [
        "",
        "## models",
        f"  {m.value_classes} value class(es) of {m.total_classes} class(es); "
        f"{m.frozen_classes} frozen ({m.frozen_ratio:.0%})",
        f"  dominant base: {m.dominant_base or '(none)'}" + (f"  bases: {bases}" if bases else ""),
        f"  config: {', '.join(f'{k}={n}' for k, n in m.config_flags) or '(none)'}",
        f"  collection fields: {m.tuple_fields} tuple / {m.list_fields} list "
        f"({m.tuple_ratio:.0%} tuple)",
    ]

cd /Users/hosanglee/archy; python3 - <<'EOF'
import json,subprocess
body="""**Bug.** `archy conventions` can name a different home module for the same family on two runs over unchanged code. Found while refactoring `cli_render.py` (code-health pass), when a before/after diff of the text output differed with no code change.

**Repro (2026-11-09, archy at 60a9fed).**
```
for seed in 1 2 3 4; do PYTHONHASHSEED=$seed uv run archy conventions . | grep -E "^  (AgentAdapter|ConventionsReport)"; done
```
`AgentAdapter 6 @` printed `archy.install.base`, `archy.install.adapters.claude`, `archy.install.adapters.continue_`, `archy.install.adapters.continue_` for seeds 1 to 4, and `ConventionsReport 2 @` printed `archy.mcp_payloads` three times and `archy.conventions` once. The top-line counts did not change, only the "@ home" module.

**Cause.** `_home_module` (`src/archy/conventions.py`) breaks ties with `Counter.most_common`, which is insertion order. Its docstring says that is "whichever module the scan reached first". It is not: `_base_families` builds the Counter from `names`, a `set` of class names, so the order is string-hash order and changes per process. (`_registries` builds its Counter from a list, so it is stable; `_surface_families` has no home.)

**Why it matters.** The home module is the answer to "where does a new one go", which is what this command is for. An agent can be told two different homes for the same family on two calls, and any test or snapshot that pins a tied family is flaky depending on the hash seed. This is the same class as #415 (one definition of home across the three family kinds) and AGENTS.md's "a verdict without a reason".

**Fix.** Break ties on `(-count, module name)` so the answer is a function of the project, not of the process. Update the docstring, which currently documents the wrong cause.

**Definition of done.**
- A test that runs the census in a subprocess under at least three `PYTHONHASHSEED` values on a fixture with a tied family and asserts the home is identical, plus the expected value worked out by hand in the docstring.
- Verified by mutation: restore the unordered tie-break, clear `__pycache__`, confirm the test goes red under at least one seed.
- Assert the fixture really has a tie before asserting the outcome (AGENTS.md, "a fixture that never reaches the branch").

**Not in scope.** Choosing a smarter home than alphabetical (for example the module defining the base). That is a product decision for a separate ticket.
"""
r=subprocess.run(["gh","api","repos/:owner/:repo/issues","--input","-"],input=json.dumps({"title":"fix(conventions): a tied family's home module depends on PYTHONHASHSEED, so the same repo gets different answers","body":body}),capture_output=True,text=True)
print(json.loads(r.stdout).get("html_url") if r.returncode==0 else r.stderr[:300])
EOF

        hint = f"  (did you mean {', '.join(suggestions[name])}?)" if name in suggestions else ""
        lines.append(f"  ! unresolved endpoint: {name}{hint}")
    for item in a.rejected:
        lines.append(f"  ! rejected: {item}")
    for note, edges in (
        ("no-op add (edge already exists)", a.no_op_adds),
        ("no-op remove (edge absent)", a.no_op_removes),
    ):
        for e in edges:
            lines.append(f"  ~ {note}: {e.source} -> {e.target}")
    return lines


def _added_block(header: str, rows: list[str]) -> list[str]:
    """A blank line, the header and the rows, or nothing when there are no rows."""
    return ["", header, *rows] if rows else []


def _simulate_added_lines(result: SimulateReport) -> list[str]:
    cycles = result.cycles.added
    back = result.new_back_edges
    violations = result.violations.added
    # Listed unconditionally, like the blocks above, NOT left to the ranked
    # summary. `simulate` has no --top-n and takes the default cap of 5, and a
    # whole-rule reach item carries risk 0.0 (it names no module to weight), so
    # it is the first thing evicted from the top-5 exactly when a simulation has
    # a lot going on. "Would removing this import break a required-reach rule?"
    # is a question simulate exists to answer; it must not depend on ranking.
    required = result.required_violations.added
    return [
        *_added_block(
            f"# new cycles (+{len(cycles)}):", [f"  + {', '.join(c.modules)}" for c in cycles]
        ),
        *_added_block(
            f"# new back-edges (+{len(back)}):", [f"  + {e.source} -> {e.target}" for e in back]
        ),
        *_added_block(
            f"# new layer violations (+{len(violations)}):",
            [
                f"  + {v.source} -> {v.target}  ({v.rule.from_layer} -> {v.rule.to_layer})"
                for v in violations
            ],
        ),
        *_added_block(
            f"# new required-reach violations (+{len(required)}):",
            [f"  + {v.detail}" for v in required],
        ),
    ]


'''
s=s[:a]+new+s[b:]
open(p,'w').write(s)
EOF

            f"({v.rule.from_layer} -> {v.rule.to_layer})"

        rule = f"{v.rule.from_layer} -> {v.rule.to_layer}"

    # A contract that could not have failed gets its own marker. Rendering

    marker = "??" if c.matched_nothing else ("OK" if c.kept else "X ")
    lines = [f"{marker} {c.name}  [{c.contract_type}]"]
    if c.matched_nothing:

            "contract holds whatever the code does"

    for expression in c.unmatched_expressions:

    for w in c.warnings:

        downstream = chain.get("downstream_module", "?")
        lines.append(f"    {downstream} -> {upstream}")
        paths = cast(list[list[dict[str, object]]], chain.get("chains") or [])

        for path in (p for p in paths if len(p) > 1):

            nodes.extend(str(step.get("imported", "?")) for step in path)

    return lines

file("docs(agents): add `cs delta main` to the pre-push checks, because CodeScene has failed PRs only after they were pushed",
"""**Lesson.** During the 2026-11-09 code-health pass CodeScene's PR check failed on real findings after the push, twice in five PRs: #865 (nested complexity in `preview_config`, from an inline block I added) and #868 (three new Deep, Nested Complexity issues in helpers I had extracted). Each cost a push, a wait of about three minutes, and a second round. A third failure (#866) was CodeScene's own "Internal error." and recovered without a change. #862, #864 and #869 passed.

**Why it is avoidable.** `cs delta main` (CodeScene CLI, installed locally) reports the same findings before pushing: per file, the old and new score, each degraded, improved and fixed issue, and the metric and threshold behind it ("cyclomatic complexity from 23 to 10, threshold = 9"). `cs check FILE` prints lint-style `warn: file:line: Smell (detail)` lines. Both ran in seconds here. See `docs/research/CODESCENE_HEALTH_MODEL.md`.

**Fix.** Add one line to the "Before you push" list in `AGENTS.md`: `cs delta main` and read the findings, with the reason above. State that it needs `cs auth` and the network, so it is a check to run when available, not a gate. Do not add it to CI: CodeScene's own PR check already runs there.

**Not in scope.** Making CodeScene a required status check (a repository-settings decision), or `--error-on-warnings` in a hook (it exits 0 by default; whether to fail on every pre-existing finding in a touched file is a separate question).

**Anti-theater.** This changes nothing about code health; it moves a failure earlier. Do not describe it as an improvement in quality.""")

file("refactor: split the six largest modules by responsibility, because function extraction cannot fix CodeScene's file-level smells",
"""**Lesson.** Splitting a long function into helpers raised `conventions.py`'s CodeScene score from 2.93 to 3.98 and `cli_render.py`'s from 3.59 to 5.08, but it did not touch the file-level smells, and it made the files longer: `cs delta` reported `conventions.py` going from 1,003 to 1,066 lines of code against a warning at 600. Those smells need the module split along a responsibility line.

**Where it stands (`cs review`, 2026-11-09, after the first two refactors).**

| module | lines | cs score | file-level smells |
|---|---|---|---|
| `cli.py` | 2,606 | 4.40 | Lines of Code in a Single File, Overall Code Complexity |
| `conventions.py` | 1,856 | 3.98 | Lines of Code in a Single File, Overall Code Complexity |
| `cli_render.py` | 1,800 | 5.08 | Low Cohesion, Overall Code Complexity |
| `mcp_runs.py` | 1,381 | 4.60 | Low Cohesion, Overall Code Complexity |
| `graph.py` | 1,365 | 4.44 | Low Cohesion, Overall Code Complexity |
| `layers.py` | 1,211 | 4.85 | Low Cohesion, Overall Code Complexity |

CodeScene's defaults: warn at 600 lines of code, alert at 3,000. Low Cohesion is LCOM4, meaning the file holds functions that share no state and do not call each other.

**Shape of the work.** One PR per module. Per module: name the responsibility lines first (for `conventions.py`: the census collectors, the surface and family builders, and the module view), split along them, and keep the public names importable from the old module so no caller changes in the same PR. Each split regenerates the derived `archy:owns` headers (`uv run archy conventions . --emit-headers --write`, never by hand) and must pass `archy check`, `archy cycles --strict` and `archy contracts`.

**Constraints from AGENTS.md.** A new module is a new node in archy's own graph: check it for a cycle and a layer violation before the PR. **Existing history.** #395 (closed) decomposed `cli` and `mcp` and removed their shared duplication; this is the next layer, driven by a measure instead of by duplication.""")

file("fix(what-to-refactor-next): every module with a hotspot row is labelled a hotspot, so tiny modules are called \"a complexity x churn hotspot\"",
"""**Bug.** `what-to-refactor-next` tells the reader that `archy.install.registry` is "Both a complexity x churn hotspot (cc_sum=5, churn=2) and a high edit-risk module", ranked 8th of 175. By `archy hotspots` it is about 156th of 175, and its CodeScene score is 10.0 (nothing to fix). `archy.risk` (cc_sum=7, churn=4) is ranked 9th with the same sentence and the same 10.0.

**Repro (archy at 60a9fed, 2026-11-09).**
```
uv run archy what-to-refactor-next . --top 12     # ranks 8 and 9 carry "hotspot+edit_risk"
uv run archy hotspots . --top 200 | grep -E "install.registry|archy.risk"
```
`archy hotspots` returns 175 rows for a 175-module project, so every module has a hotspot row.

**Cause.** In `src/archy/refactor.py` the `"hotspot"` lens is appended when `hs is not None`, that is, whenever the module has any hotspot row (`lenses.append("hotspot")`, around line 186). `candidates = set(hotspot_by_module) | risky` therefore starts as the whole project, and the label never discriminates. The structural lens has a floor (`min_risk`); the hotspot lens has none.

**Why it matters.** The label is the reason the row is shown (AGENTS.md: a verdict without a reason is not actionable; and a reason that is false is worse). An agent told to "prioritize it, both the most active and the most dangerous surface" is sent to a module with 2 commits and cc_sum 5. It also pushes the actually worst file down: `archy.conventions`, the churn-16, cs-score-2.93 file, was 14th.

**Fix.** Give the hotspot lens a floor of its own, in the way the structural lens has `min_risk`: for example only the top fraction of hotspot scores, or a score at or above a stated share of the maximum. Choose it by looking at the distribution on the bench projects, not by taste, and state the cut in the docstring. A module below the floor keeps its rank but loses the word "hotspot" from its row.

**Definition of done.**
- A test on a hand-built graph where one module is a real hotspot and several others have a hotspot row with trivial scores, asserting only the real one carries the `hotspot` lens and the prose. Assert the fixture has the trivial rows before asserting the outcome.
- Verified by mutation: restore the unconditional `lenses.append("hotspot")`, clear `__pycache__`, confirm red.
- All three surfaces checked (`_refactor_to_text`, the JSON, the MCP return model), per AGENTS.md. The wording is rendered in `cli_render.py` and `mcp_runs.py` (`_refactor_note`).

**Related, not in scope.** Whether the ranking should add a smell or health term (#871, #870). This ticket only makes the existing label true.""")

## Why orthogonality is necessary but not sufficient

A random number generator would be orthogonal to the existing axes. So would "alphabetical position of the package name." So would "number of files starting with an underscore." Statistical independence is a hygiene check against double-counting; it is not evidence the signal measures architectural quality.

The composite-indicator literature (OECD Handbook, JRC reports) is explicit on this.[^oecd] A sub-indicator must satisfy **four** conditions to belong in a quality composite:

1. **Independence** (orthogonality). `calls_per_edge` passes.
2. **Directionality.** There must be a defensible answer to "is higher better, or worse?" that holds across the population.
3. **Actionability.** There must be a refactoring action a practitioner can take to improve the indicator that is independently considered good practice.
4. **Discriminant validity.** The indicator must distinguish projects that domain experts consider better-architected from those they consider worse-architected.

`calls_per_edge` fails conditions 2, 3, and 4.

### Condition 2: directionality is shape-driven, not quality-driven

The top of the distribution (numpy, pygments, mkdocs, mypy, scikit-learn) is dominated by scientific-Python and AST-heavy tools. The bottom (starlette, scrapy, flask, boto3) is web frameworks and auto-generated SDKs that score well on archy's own axes (boto3 0.653, starlette 0.610, scrapy 0.606). The point is that the bottom of 

The signal is correlated with **codebase shape**, not **codebase health**. The strongest direct evidence is that `calls_per_edge` barely correlates with archy's own composite at all: across the 28-project bench, **Pearson `r = -0.03`, Spearman `+0.18`** between `calls_per_edge` and `overall`. A would-be quality axis that is stat

- High `calls_per_edge` is caused by intra-module function dispatch (numpy's ndarray methods route through a handful of internal modules; mypy's analysis pipeline runs many narrow passes against the same nodes).
- Low `calls_per_edge` is caused by registry, plugin, and dynamic-dispatch patterns (starlette's middleware chain; scrapy's component registry; boto3's auto-generated SDK; msgspec's typed-dispatch shortcut).

Neither shape is intrinsically bad. [`RESEARCH_METRICS.md` section 16](RESEARCH_METRICS.md) itself observes this:

> "Scientific Python tops the distribution. The 'shape' of these codebases - small core, broad call surface against it - is exactly what the call signal captures and the import signal misses."

#!/usr/bin/env python
"""Pull the whole distribution funnel in one command and append a dated row.

Nine research documents defer candidates "behind a usage signal" without that
phrase having a source, a cadence, or a threshold. This script is the source
and the cadence; ``docs/DISTRIBUTION.md`` is the threshold.

Why a script and not the hand-run curl commands in ``docs/PYPI_STATS.md``:

  - **The GitHub traffic endpoints keep a 14-day rolling window.** Views,
    clones, referrers, and paths older than 14 days are gone permanently, for
    everyone, with no archive to recover them from. A month you forget to pull
    is a month that never existed. That alone justifies automating it.
  - **pypistats rate-limits aggressively.** During the #316 research it
    returned HTTP 429 and the download figure simply could not be reported.
    Every source here retries with backoff and, if it still fails, records an
    explicit ``null`` plus the error string rather than crashing the run or
    silently reporting a stale number as current.

No telemetry, by design. Every source below is external and public: archy
itself never phones home, and ``docs/INSTALL.md`` promises exactly that. The
marginal fidelity of in-process metrics is not worth trading that promise for.

Rows are raw counts only, never derived percentages or ratios. Percentages
bake in an interpretation that cannot be undone later; counts can always be
re-analyzed against a question nobody has thought to ask yet.

Usage:
    uv run python bench/distribution.py                    # append a row
    uv run python bench/distribution.py --dry-run          # print, don't append

The GitHub traffic endpoints are owner-only and need a token with repo scope.
The script reads ``GITHUB_TOKEN`` / ``GH_TOKEN``, else falls back to
``gh auth token``. Without one it degrades cleanly: every other source still
lands and the traffic block records its null.

archy:owns        append, build_row, main, pull_adopters, pull_community, pull_pypi,
                  pull_repo, pull_traffic, summarize
"""

"""Shared helpers for the bench sweep scripts.

Extracted so `hotspots_sweep.py` and `duplicates_sweep.py` (and any future
sweep) share one manifest loader and one clone/checkout routine instead of
copy-pasting them. Sweep scripts are run as `python bench/<name>.py`, so
`bench/` is on `sys.path[0]` and this module imports as `from _common import ...`.

archy:owns        clone_or_update, load_manifest
"""

from __future__ import annotations

import subprocess
from pathlib import Path

import yaml  # type: ignore[import-untyped]

REPO_ROOT = Path(__file__).resolve().parent.parent
MANIFEST = REPO_ROOT / "bench" / "projects.yaml"
WORKDIR = Path("/tmp/archy_bench")


def load_manifest() -> list[dict]:
    return yaml.safe_load(MANIFEST.read_text())["projects"]


def clone_or_update(proj: dict) -> Path | None:
    """Clone/checkout a project at its pinned SHA; never raises -- on any failure
    return None so the caller can skip the project and keep the sweep going. The
    archy self-entry uses REPO_ROOT directly (its pin may name a tag that does
    not exist yet during a release PR)."""
    name = proj["name"]
    sha = proj["sha"]
    if name == "archy":
        return REPO_ROOT
    target = WORKDIR / name
    if not target.exists():
        WORKDIR.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
        res = subprocess.run(
            ["git", "clone", "--quiet", f"https://github.com/{proj['repo']}.git", str(target)],
        )
        if res.returncode != 0:
            return None
    has_sha = subprocess.run(
        ["git", "-C", str(target), "cat-file", "-e", sha],
        capture_output=True,
    )
    if has_sha.returncode != 0:
        subprocess.run(["git", "-C", str(target), "fetch", "--quiet", "origin"], check=False)
    if (
        subprocess.run(
            ["git", "-C", str(target), "checkout", "--quiet", sha],
        ).returncode
        != 0
    ):
        return None
    subprocess.run(["git", "-C", str(target), "reset", "--hard", "--quiet", sha], check=False)
    subprocess.run(["git", "-C", str(target), "clean", "-fdx", "--quiet"], check=False)
    return target

input.command:
cd /Users/hosanglee/archy; git checkout -q -b alee/health-repro-prereg; cat > docs/research/HEALTH_REPRODUCIBILITY_PREREG.md <<'EOF'
# Pre-registration: can archy reproduce CodeScene's per-function smells? (#870)

Committed 2026-11-09, **before any run over the bench corpus**. Thresholds below
are fixed. A result that misses one is written up as a miss; none is
reinterpreted afterwards.

Background and sources: [`CODESCENE_HEALTH_MODEL.md`](CODESCENE_HEALTH_MODEL.md).
Ticket: #870. The decision it feeds: whether `archy health` (#871) ships, and
which detectors it ships with.

## Question

For each of six function-level smells, does a detector built on archy's own
parse flag the same functions that `cs review` flags, on real projects? And does
a per-file count of those smells track `cs`'s file score?

## What is and is not claimed

A hit licenses only "archy reports the same flagged functions as `cs`". It does
not license "healthier code", fewer defects, or better agent runs, and it is not
a case for a score axis (that has its own gate, recorded on #870). The reference
is a vendor tool whose own validity this repository has not checked.

## Detector definitions

Read from `cs rules-config list-thresholds --language python` and fixed by the
calibration probes below. The calibration is not a result; it only settles what
each detector means, so the comparison is not lost to a definition mismatch.

| Smell | archy-side rule | Settled by calibration |
|---|---|---|
| Complex Method | `archy.complexity` cyclomatic at or above 9 | threshold from `cs` |
| Excess Arguments | more than 4 parameters, **excluding `self` and `cls`**, counting `*args`, `**kwargs` and keyword-only | `self` and `cls` not counted; the other three counted |
| Large Method | more than 70 **code** lines, counting docstring lines, excluding blank and comment-only lines | blanks and comments not counted; docstrings counted |
| Deep Nesting | nesting depth of 4 or more through `if`, `for`, `while` only | four nested `for` fires; `with`/`try` and `elif` chains do not; comprehension filters do not |
| Complex Conditional | two or more boolean operators in an `if` or `while` condition | `return a and b and c` and assignments do not fire; `if a and b or c` does |
| Bumpy Road | **not in this round** | the definition (what separates two bumps) was not recoverable from probes |

Two calibration surprises recorded rather than papered over: a nested function
with five parameters was not flagged by `cs`, and a nested class method was not
checked either way. The detector follows `cs` (top-level functions and methods
only) so the comparison is like for like; whether archy should differ is a
separate decision.

## Data

- Projects: every entry in `bench/projects.yaml`, cloned at its pinned SHA by
  `bench/_common.clone_or_update`.
- Files: tracked `*.py`, excluding any path with a `tests`, `test`, `docs`,
  `examples`, `migrations` or `vendor` segment. The unit is the function,
  identified by (file, name, line).
- Files `cs review` returns a null score for are **dropped, never counted as
  clean** (AGENTS.md).
- Pilot: `archy` itself plus two small projects, to catch harness bugs only. The
  pilot is excluded from the result and may not change any threshold below.
- Cost guard: a project is skipped, and listed as skipped with the reason, if
  `cs review` over its files exceeds 30 minutes. A skipped project is not
  scored as agreeing.

## Matching

A flagged function on one side matches the other when it has the same file and
the same name. If a name is not unique in the file, the nearest start line
within 3 lines. Decorated functions start on the decorator line in one tool and
the `def` line in the other, which is what the 3-line window is for. An
unmatched flag counts against agreement on the side that has it.

## Measures

1. **Per-smell flag-set agreement:** Jaccard index of flagged functions,
   pooled over all projects, plus each project's own index reported beside it.
2. **File-level agreement:** Spearman rank correlation between archy's
   per-file count of flagged functions (all five detectors) and `cs`'s file
   score, pooled over files with a score, plus the per-project median.

## Thresholds, fixed now

- A detector is **reproducible** when pooled Jaccard is at least **0.80**.
- A file measure is **reproducible** when pooled Spearman is at most **-0.80**
  (more archy smells, lower `cs` score).
- If pooled Spearman is between -0.70 and -0.80, say it is not reproducible, and
  ship individual detectors only.
- If it is above -0.70, do not ship a file-level number at all.
- Complex Method is already measured on archy's own `src/` (2026-11-09, outside
  the corpus): Jaccard 92 / (112 + 109 - 92) = 0.71. That is a baseline, not a
  result, and it is below the bar.

## What would change the plan

- Fewer than **four** detectors reach 0.80: ship `archy health` with only those
  that did, and say plainly which smells it does not report.
- Complex Method fails because the two tools count different constructs: say
  which, then decide whether to match `cs` or document the difference. Do not
  quietly adopt `cs`'s count to pass the bar.
- Results differ between large and small projects by more than 0.15 in Jaccard:
  report both and do not pool.

## Threats, stated up front

- archy's cyclomatic comes from tree-sitter; the other detectors in the
  prototype use Python's `ast`. A shipped detector that uses tree-sitter
  throughout could differ.
- `cs` may change thresholds between releases. The version string is recorded
  in the result.
- Agreement with `cs` is not agreement with anything else. If it is high, that
  is evidence the detectors are not buggy, not evidence they measure quality.

## Calibration record (2026-11-09, `cs review` on synthetic files)

| Probe | Result |
|---|---|
| method with `self` + 4 parameters | not flagged |
| method with `self` + 5 parameters | flagged, "Arguments = 5" |
| `cls` + 4 parameters (classmethod) | not flagged |
| `a, b, c, *args, **kwargs` | flagged, "Arguments = 5" |
| `a, b, *, c, d, e` (keyword-only) | flagged, "Arguments = 5" |
| nested function, 5 parameters | not flagged |
| 40 statements separated by blank lines | not flagged |
| 40 statements each preceded by a comment | not flagged |
| 70-line docstring | flagged, "LoC = 72 lines" |
| four nested `for` | flagged, "Nesting depth = 4" |
| `for`, `while`, `with`, `try`/`except` nested | not flagged |
| five-branch `elif` chain | not flagged |
| comprehension with four `if` filters | not flagged |
| `return a and b and c`, `x = a and b and c` | not flagged |
| `if a and b and c`, `if a and b or c`, `while a and b and c` | flagged, "2 complex conditional expressions" |
| `if not a and not b` | not flagged |
EOF

"body":"""**Bug.** `bench/_common.clone_or_update` returns `None` on any of four different failures (the clone, the fetch of a missing pin, the checkout, and now the unshallow) and prints nothing about which. Callers record the project as skipped with a generic reason.

**Found by.** The #870 reproducibility run (2026-11-09). `fastapi` was recorded `{"status": "error", "reason": "clone failed"}`, yet its pin `c61384e` is present once the clone is unshallowed (`git fetch --unshallow origin`, then `git cat-file -e c61384e` succeeds; the clone is on `master` at 7,997 commits). The row cannot say whether the clone failed, the fetch timed out, or the checkout was refused, so there is nothing to act on except re-running.

**Why it matters.** AGENTS.md: a verdict without a reason is not actionable, and for a bench, a project silently missing from a result is a biased sample. The same helper is shared by every sweep (`hotspots_sweep`, `duplicates_sweep`, and others), so each of them can drop a project with no cause recorded.

**Fix.** Return a result that carries the failing step and git's stderr (a small frozen dataclass or a raised error with the step named), have callers write it into the ledger row's `reason`, and keep the documented "never raises" contract at the call sites that need it. Keep `None`-returning behaviour for callers that rely on it only if a grep shows any do.

**Definition of done.** A test with a stub `git` (or a bare local repository) for each of the four failures asserting the reason names the step. Verified by mutation: collapse two failures into one reason and confirm red.

"body":"""**Ask (2026-11-09).** archy should give a pull request author the kind of feedback CodeScene's PR check gives. Concretely, from what CodeScene did on this repository's PRs (#865, #868, #881): an **inline comment on the function's line** naming the smell and the measured value ("main has a cyclomatic complexity of 11"), one comment per new issue, only for issues the PR introduced, plus a **gate summary check** ("Quality Gate Passed"). #868 and #881 each failed that check on new code and could be fixed from the comments alone.

**What archy has today.** `.github/workflows/score-delta.yml` and `score-comment.yml` post the score delta as a comment (#604, still open). `archy diff` already carries a file and line range for every new layer violation (`v.path`, `v.lines`; see `_diff_violation_lines` in `cli_render.py`) and names the rule. Nothing puts a finding on the diff.

**Mechanism that needs no bot and no write token.** GitHub workflow commands (`::error file=F,line=N,title=T::message`) become annotations on the PR's Files tab from a read-only job. The existing design already keeps the PR-code job read-only because a fork's token cannot write (`score-delta.yml`); annotations fit that constraint where a posted comment does not. GitHub caps annotations per step and per job; check the current limit before sizing, and design for hitting it.

**Phase 1 (no dependency).** Add `--format github` to `archy diff` and `archy check` (CLI only; the MCP tools already return structured findings and do not need a workflow-command format, say so in the PR). For each new layer violation, new required-reach violation and new cycle, emit one annotation at the import line (violations) or the module's path (cycles), with the rule and the before and after. Wire the Action's `diff` and `check` commands to use it.

**Phase 2 (blocked on #871 and #872).** The same output for new smells: one annotation per new smell at the function's line, with the metric and threshold ("cyclomatic complexity 12, threshold 9"), limited to lines the PR touched, as `cs delta` limits itself to changed files.

**Rules from AGENTS.md that apply.**
- **A verdict without a reason is not actionable.** Every annotation carries the rule or smell, the measured value, and the threshold or rule it broke.
- **Never truncate silently.** When the cap is reached, the last annotation says how many were not shown and the job summary lists them all. A PR that looks clean because the annotations ran out is the failure to avoid.
- **A name that matched nothing is a refusal.** A finding with no resolvable line is still reported, in the summary, not dropped.
- **Test the serialized form.** Assert the exact workflow-command text, including the escaping GitHub requires for `%`, `\\r`, `\\n` in the message and `,` and `:` in properties; a message with a newline or a path with a comma must not break the command. Mutation-verify the escaping.
- **Wire it to every surface in one change**, or state why a surface is exempt.

**Anti-theater.** The annotation reports a finding; it does not claim the code got better or worse for a human or an agent. The Phase 2 numbers carry whatever validity #870 finds and no more.

**Not in scope.** Posting review comments through the API (needs a write token; that is #604's sticky-comment path), auto-fix suggestions, and a quality-gate pass/fail policy (#872).

**Related.** #604 (summary and comment surface; design together so one summary carries both), #607 (script injection in the Action's shell inputs: annotation text built from PR-controlled strings must be escaped, so this ticket must not land before #607 is understood), #871, #872."""})

body="""**Question (asked 2026-11-09).** Should archy's per-function cyclomatic complexity count the way CodeScene's does?

**Finding.** `src/archy/complexity.py` documents that archy's count is radon-compatible on purpose (`assert` excluded "to match radon's default"; comprehension `for` and `if` counted separately "matching radon"). CodeScene's differs. Measured with `cs check`, which prints its own value, on synthetic functions with 12 of one construct each (a function with none of the construct is cc 1; a result of 13 means each instance counted once):

| construct, 12 times | CodeScene | archy |
|---|---|---|
| `if`, `elif`, `for`, `while`, `except` clause, `and`/`or` operand | counted (13) | counted (13) |
| comprehension `for` | counted once (13) | counted once (13) |
| comprehension `if` (list, dict, generator) | counted once (13) | **counted twice** (25) |
| `raise` (12 `if`s each with a `raise`) | **counted** (25) | not counted (13) |
| conditional expression (`a if b else c`) | **not counted** (below 9) | counted (13) |
| `match` / `case` | **not counted** (below 9) | counted (14) |
| ternary inside a lambda | **not counted** (below 9) | counted (13) |
| `assert`, `with`, `lambda` alone, `try`/`else`/`finally` | not counted | not counted |
| `return`, `break` | not counted | not counted |

`raise` counting is the largest effect: validators and parsers full of `raise` are flagged by CodeScene and not by archy, and comprehension-heavy code is the reverse.

**Effect on the #870 comparison (exploratory, post hoc).** Pooled Complex Method agreement over the 26 bench projects was 0.673 (the pre-registered result, below the 0.80 bar). Recomputing archy's flags with a CodeScene-style count (1 + `if`/`elif`, loops, `except`, boolean operands, comprehension `for`, and `raise`; not comprehension `if`, ternary, `match` or lambda) gives **0.849** (archy 12,490 flagged, CodeScene 13,452, both 11,908). The rule was written from the synthetic probes above before it was run on the corpus, not fitted to the corpus; about 0.15 of disagreement is still unexplained. This does not change the pre-registered outcome.

**Effect on archy's own number (exploratory).** Across the same 26 projects and 185,499 top-level functions, the project-level mean cyclomatic moves between 0.989x and 1.155x (median 1.063x). Project order barely changes (Spearman 0.982), but only 3 of the 5 most complex projects stay the same. 1. Keep the radon-compatible count everywhere. `archy health` reports Complex Method as not reproducible against CodeScene, per the pre-registration, and says so.

def compute_conventions(
    root: Path,
    *,
    ignored_dirs: Iterable[str] = DEFAULT_IGNORED_DIRS,
    extra_roots: Iterable[str] = (),
    min_family: int = 2,
    include_tests: bool = False,
) -> ConventionsReport:
    """Derive `root`'s house style from its own source.

    `min_family` is the floor for reporting a naming family or a mirrored
    surface set: at 2 a single pair counts, which is the right default for
    a small project and noisy on a large one.
    """
    modules = list(discover_modules(root, ignored_dirs=ignored_dirs, extra_roots=extra_roots))
    # 🔴 Partition BEFORE parsing, and report what was set aside. A census run
    # over tests and vendored copies answers a different question from the one
    # asked; see ModulePartition for the measured failure that motivated this.
    shadows = _shadow_roots(m.qualname for m in modules)
    counts: Counter[str] = Counter()
    kept = []
    for module in modules:
        bucket, _ = _classify_module(module.qualname, shadows, include_tests=include_tests)
        counts[bucket] += 1
        if bucket == "censused":
            kept.append(module)
    n_tests, n_shadowed, n_nonsource = (
        counts["test"],
        counts["shadowed"],
        counts["nonsource"],
    )
    modules = kept
    facts: list[_ModuleFacts] = []
    skipped: list[UnparsedModule] = []
    for module in modules:
        collected, miss = _try_collect_detailed(module, root=root)
        if collected is None:
            assert miss is not None
            skipped.append(miss)
            continue
        facts.append(collected)

    gates, errors = _gates(facts)
    bases = _base_families(facts, min_count=min_family)
    registries = _registries(facts, min_count=min_family)
    docs, docs_seen = _harvest_docs(root, frozenset(ignored_dirs))
    return ConventionsReport(
        root=str(root),
        modules_scanned=len(facts),
        modules_unparsed=len(skipped),
        unparsed_modules=tuple(skipped),
        naming=_naming_families(facts, min_count=min_family),
        surfaces=_surface_families(facts, min_count=min_family),
        gates=gates,
        errors=errors,
        models=_model_census(facts),
        bases=bases,
        registries=registries,
        export_gaps=_export_gaps(facts, bases),
        doc_gaps=_doc_gaps(bases, registries, docs),
        docs_scanned=docs_seen,
        partition=ModulePartition(
            production=len(facts),
            tests=n_tests,
            shadowed=n_shadowed,
            nonsource=n_nonsource,
            shadow_roots=tuple(sorted(shadows)),
        ),
    )


def compute_module_view(
    root: Path,
    module: str,
    *,
    ignored_dirs: Iterable[str] = DEFAULT_IGNORED_DIRS,
    extra_roots: Iterable[str] = (),
    include_tests: bool = False,
) -> ModuleView:
    """The complete, unranked picture of one module. See ModuleView.

    Note that this parses EVERY module regardless of `include_tests`, because
    "who imports me" is a question about the whole project: a module imported
    only by tests is imported, and reporting it as unused because tests were set
    aside would be a false negative of exactly the kind this function exists to
    prevent. `include_tests` decides `status`, not the search.
    """
    modules = list(discover_modules(root, ignored_dirs=ignored_dirs, extra_roots=extra_roots))
    shadows = _shadow_roots(m.qualname for m in modules)

    facts: dict[str, _ModuleFacts] = {}
    skipped: list[UnparsedModule] = []
    for m in modules:
        collected, miss = _try_collect_detailed(m, root=root)
        if collected is None:
            assert miss is not None
            skipped.append(miss)
            continue
        facts[m.qualname] = collected
    unparsed = tuple(skipped)

    if module not in facts:
        miss = next((u for u in unparsed if u.module == module), None)
        if miss is not None:
            # The module exists on disk but this interpreter cannot census it.
            # Returning a view (not LookupError) keeps the negative answerable:
            # the lists are empty because parsing failed, not because the name
            # is unknown (#666).
            return ModuleView(
                module=module,
                status=(f"could not be parsed (Python {miss.python}): {miss.reason} ({miss.path})"),
                classes=(),
                functions=(),
                imports_internal=(),
                imported_by=(),
                exports=None,
                suffix_families=(),
                gates=(),
                census_complete=False,
                unparsed_modules=(miss,),
            )
        near = suggest_modules(facts, module)
        # Also suggest unparsed names: an agent asking for pkg.cache after a
        # SyntaxError skip must not be told the module does not exist.
        near_unparsed = [u.module for u in unparsed if module.split(".")[-1] in u.module]
        suggestions = list(dict.fromkeys([*near, *near_unparsed]))
        raise LookupError(
            f"no module {module!r} under {root}"
            + (f"; did you mean {', '.join(suggestions[:5])}?" if suggestions else "")
        )

    f = facts[module]
    known = frozenset(facts)
    reexports = _reexport_maps(facts, known)
    resolved = {q: _resolved_imports(g, known, reexports) for q, g in facts.items()}
    # Complete on both sides. A "does X import Y" question is answered by the
    # presence or ABSENCE of Y here, so a partial list is worse than none.
    # When any module was unparsed, that completeness claim is false (#666).
    imports = sorted(resolved[module] - {module})
    by = sorted(q for q, mods in resolved.items() if q != module and module in mods)
    fams = sorted({camel_suffix(c.name) for c in f.classes})
    gates, errors = _gates([f])
    return ModuleView(
        module=module,
        status=_classify_module(module, shadows, include_tests=include_tests)[1],
        classes=tuple(sorted(c.name for c in f.classes)),
        functions=tuple(sorted(fn.name for fn in f.functions)),
        imports_internal=tuple(imports),
        imported_by=tuple(by),
        exports=tuple(sorted(f.exports)) if f.exports is not None else None,
        suffix_families=tuple(fams),
        gates=tuple(gates) + tuple(errors),
        census_complete=not unparsed,
        unparsed_modules=unparsed,
    )

        if miss is not None:
            # The module exists on disk but this interpreter cannot census it.
            # Returning a view (not LookupError) keeps the negative answerable:
            # the lists are empty because parsing failed, not because the name
            # is unknown (#666).
            return ModuleView(
                module=module,
                status=(f"could not be parsed (Python {miss.python}): {miss.reason} ({miss.path})"),
                classes=(),
                functions=(),
                imports_internal=(),
                imported_by=(),
                exports=None,
                suffix_families=(),
                gates=(),
                census_complete=False,
                unparsed_modules=(miss,),
            )
        near = suggest_modules(facts, module)

        # SyntaxError skip must not be told the module does not exist.
        near_unparsed = [u.module for u in unparsed if module.split(".")[-1] in u.module]
        suggestions = list(dict.fromkeys([*near, *near_unparsed]))

            f"no module {module!r} under {root}"
            + (f"; did you mean {', '.join(suggestions[:5])}?" if suggestions else "")

    known = frozenset(facts)
    reexports = _reexport_maps(facts, known)
    resolved = {q: _resolved_imports(g, known, reexports) for q, g in facts.items()}

    # presence or ABSENCE of Y here, so a partial list is worse than none.
    # When any module was unparsed, that completeness claim is false (#666).
    imports = sorted(resolved[module] - {module})
    by = sorted(q for q, mods in resolved.items() if q != module and module in mods)
    fams = sorted({camel_suffix(c.name) for c in f.classes})
    gates, errors = _gates([f])
    return ModuleView(
        module=module,
        status=_classify_module(module, shadows, include_tests=include_tests)[1],
        classes=tuple(sorted(c.name for c in f.classes)),
        functions=tuple(sorted(fn.name for fn in f.functions)),
        imports_internal=tuple(imports),
        imported_by=tuple(by),
        exports=tuple(sorted(f.exports)) if f.exports is not None else None,
        suffix_families=tuple(fams),
        gates=tuple(gates) + tuple(errors),
        census_complete=not unparsed,
        unparsed_modules=unparsed,
    )

    """The names one package re-exports, each mapped to the submodule it came from."""
    pkg_map: dict[str, str] = {}
    for base, names in f.import_froms:
        # Only a SELF-referential import re-exports. `graph._reexport_source`
        # skips anything else, on the grounds that re-exporting a module from
        # outside the package says nothing about where the package's own names
        # live; treating it as a re-export routed `from pkgA import Thing` to
        # `pkgB.impl` and reported nothing importing `pkgA`, where the graph
        # reports the `pkgA` edge. A relative import always lands inside the
        # package by construction, so this one check covers both forms.
        if base != qualname and not base.startswith(qualname + "."):
            continue
        # `from .x import y` re-exports `y` from the submodule `x`, always.
        # Whether `x.y` is a module or a symbol `x` defines is not in the
        # syntax: Python prefers the attribute, so a symbol `y` shadows a

        # the program never makes (#436). `x` is an edge in both cases.
